docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
Computing is one of humanity’s greatest achievements, yet for most people, it remains mysterious. We type code on keyboards, click buttons on screens, and somehow our intentions become reality through an invisible process involving billions of microscopic switches.

This book demystifies that process. We follow a simple addition operation through twelve distinct stages of transformation, from the high-level code you write to the electrons flowing through silicon transistors. Each stage represents decades of engineering innovation and human ingenuity.

Our journey spans multiple disciplines: software engineering, computer architecture, digital logic design, semiconductor physics, and quantum mechanics. Yet we present it all in an accessible way, with plenty of examples, analogies, and visual aids.

Whether you’re a student learning computer science, a software developer curious about what happens "under the hood," or simply someone fascinated by how our digital world works, this book will give you a deep appreciation for the engineering marvel that is modern computing.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: The Magic Behind Code Execution
docs.text:
When you type print("Hello, World!") in Python and see the output on your screen, you’ve just witnessed one of the most remarkable chains of transformation in modern technology. Your simple, human-readable instruction has traveled through multiple layers of abstraction, been translated by sophisticated software, loaded into memory, and finally executed by billions of microscopic switches moving electrons in precise patterns.

This seemingly magical process involves a complex journey through twelve distinct stages, each representing decades of engineering innovation. Our goal in this book is to demystify this journey completely, taking you from the code you write to the electrons that flow through silicon.

docs.title: 1.1 The Computing Stack: Layers of Abstraction
docs.text:
Modern computing systems are built as a stack of abstractions, where each layer hides the complexity of the layers below it. This design principle allows software developers to write programs without needing to understand quantum physics, and allows physicists to design transistors without needing to understand software algorithms.

Figure 1.1. The Computing Stack: Layers of Abstraction

docs.title: 1.2 Our Journey: From High-Level Code to Electrons
docs.text:
This book follows a simple addition operation through all twelve stages of transformation:

#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    int a = 15;
    int b = 25;
    int result = a + b;
    printf("The result is:
    return 0;
}

We’ll focus particularly on the line int result = a + b; and trace how this simple addition becomes a physical reality involving electrons moving through transistors.

docs.title: 1.2.1 The Twelve Stages
docs.text:
Our journey encompasses twelve distinct stages, which we can group into three major phases:

Figure 1.2. The Three Phases of Our Journey

Key Takeaway

Key Insight: These three phases happen at different times:

  • Hardware Design: Happened years ago when engineers designed your CPU

  • Build Time: Happens when you compile your program

  • Runtime: Happens every time you run your program

Your simple addition operation leverages work done by thousands of engineers across decades!

docs.title: 1.4 What Makes This Journey Remarkable
docs.text: Several aspects make the code-to-electrons journey extraordinary:

docs.title: 1.4.1 Scale and Precision
docs.text: Modern processors contain billions of transistors, each smaller than a virus, switching billions of times per second with atomic precision. Yet they work reliably for years.

docs.title: 1.4.2 Speed
docs.text:
From the moment you press "Enter" to when you see output, your code travels through all twelve stages in microseconds. This involves:

  • Operating system scheduling (microseconds)

  • CPU instruction execution (nanoseconds)

  • Transistor switching (picoseconds)

  • Electron movement (femtoseconds)

docs.title: 1.4.3 Abstraction Layers
docs.text: Each layer hides complexity while enabling functionality. A Python programmer doesn’t need to understand semiconductor physics, yet their code ultimately depends on quantum mechanical effects.

docs.title: 1.4.4 Collaborative Achievement
docs.text:
Your simple program works because of contributions from:

  • Language designers (Python, C, Java creators)

  • Compiler engineers (GCC, LLVM teams)

  • Operating system developers (Linux, Windows teams)

  • CPU architects (Intel, AMD, ARM designers)

  • Chip designers (Layout and verification engineers)

  • Fabrication engineers (Semiconductor manufacturing)

  • Physicists and materials scientists

Practical Example

The Scale of Modern Computing:

Let’s put the numbers in perspective for a modern smartphone:

  • Transistors:  15 billion (more than twice the number of people on Earth)

  • Size: 5 nanometer process (50 atoms wide)

  • Speed: 3 GHz (3 billion operations per second)

  • Power:  5 watts (less than a small light bulb)

  • Cost:  $400 (cheaper than most textbooks per transistor)

Your pocket contains more computing power than entire universities had in the 1980s!

docs.title: 1.5 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
In this introduction, we’ve established our mission: to understand how simple code becomes physical reality through twelve stages of transformation. We’ve outlined the three major phases (build time, runtime, hardware design) and set expectations for our learning journey.

The next chapter begins our exploration with the most familiar stage - writing high-level code. We’ll examine what makes programming languages "high-level" and why this abstraction is so powerful.

Remember: every expert was once a beginner. The computing stack represents one of humanity’s greatest intellectual achievements, built by thousands of brilliant people over decades. You’re about to join the ranks of those who truly understand how our digital world works.

docs.title: Chapter 2: High-Level Programming Languages: Where It All Begins
docs.text: Every computing journey begins with an idea expressed in a programming language. This chapter explores how high-level languages serve as the bridge between human thought and machine execution. We’ll examine what makes a language "high-level," how different paradigms approach problem-solving, and why abstraction is computing’s most powerful tool.

docs.title: 2.1 What Makes a Language "High-Level"?
docs.text:
A high-level programming language abstracts away the details of the computer’s architecture, allowing programmers to express ideas in terms closer to human thinking rather than machine operations.

Figure 2.1. The Abstraction Hierarchy in Programming

docs.title: 1. Human-Readable Syntax
docs.text:
High-level languages use English-like keywords and mathematical notation:

if temperature > 30:
    print("It's hot today!")
    turn_on_air_conditioning()
else:
    print("The weather is comfortable.")

Compare this to the equivalent assembly code:

MOV  EAX, [temperature]
    CMP  EAX, 30
    JLE  else_branch
    PUSH offset msg_hot
    CALL printf
    CALL turn_on_ac
    JMP  end_if
else_branch:
    PUSH offset msg_comfortable
    CALL printf
end_if:

docs.title: 2. Automatic Memory Management
docs.text:
High-level languages handle memory allocation and deallocation automatically:

// Java handles memory automatically
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Alice");    // Memory allocated automatically
names.add("Bob");      // List grows as needed
// Garbage collector will free memory when done

// C requires explicit memory management
char** names = (char**)malloc(2 * sizeof(char*));
names[0] = (char*)malloc(6 * sizeof(char));
strcpy(names[0], "Alice");
names[1] = (char*)malloc(4 * sizeof(char));
strcpy(names[1], "Bob");
// Must explicitly free memory
free(names[0]);
free(names[1]);
free(names);

docs.title: 3. Abstract Data Types
docs.text:
High-level languages provide rich data structures that model real-world concepts:

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, age, grades):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age
        self.grades = grades

    def calculate_gpa(self):
        return sum(self.grades) / len(self.grades)

# Using the abstraction
student = Student("Alice", 20, [85, 90, 88, 92])
print(f"{student.name}'s GPA: {student.calculate_gpa()}")

docs.title: 2.2 Programming Paradigms
docs.text: Different high-level languages embrace different paradigms - fundamental styles of programming that shape how we structure and think about code.

docs.title: 2.2.1 Imperative Programming
docs.text:
Programs are sequences of commands that change state:

int factorial(int n) {
    int result = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        result = result * i;  // Explicitly change state
    }
    return result;
}

docs.title: 2.2.2 Functional Programming
docs.text:
Programs are compositions of mathematical functions without side effects:

# Recursive, no state changes
def factorial(n):
    return 1 if n == 0 else n * factorial(n - 1)

# Using higher-order functions
from functools import reduce
import operator

def factorial_functional(n):
    return reduce(operator.mul, range(1, n + 1), 1)

docs.title: 2.2.3 Object-Oriented Programming
docs.text:
Programs are collections of interacting objects:

public class Calculator {
    private List<Integer> history;

    public Calculator() {
        this.history = new ArrayList<>();
    }

    public int factorial(int n) {
        int result = 1;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            result *= i;
        }
        history.add(result);  // Track calculations
        return result;
    }

    public List<Integer> getHistory() {
        return new ArrayList<>(history);  // Return copy
    }
}

docs.title: 2.2.4 Declarative Programming
docs.text:
Programs specify what should be done, not how:

-- SQL: Declare what we want, not how to get it
SELECT students.name, AVG(grades.score) as gpa
FROM students
JOIN grades ON students.id = grades.student_id
WHERE students.year = 2024
GROUP BY students.name
HAVING AVG(grades.score) > 3.5
ORDER BY gpa DESC;

Real-World Analogy

Think of programming paradigms like different ways to give directions:

  • Imperative: "Walk 100 meters, turn left, walk 50 meters, enter the building"

  • Functional: "The destination is the result of applying these transformations to your current position"

  • Object-Oriented: "Ask the Navigator object to guide you using its findPath method"

  • Declarative: "I need to be at the coffee shop on Main Street"

docs.title: 2.3 Our Example Program: Multiple Perspectives
docs.text: Let’s implement our addition example in different languages to see how each expresses the same concept:

docs.title: 2.3.1 Python - Dynamic and Simple
docs.text:
# Python emphasizes readability
def add_numbers(a, b):
    """Add two numbers and return the result."""
    return a + b

# Dynamic typing - no type declarations needed
a = 15
b = 25
result = add_numbers(a, b)
print(f"The result is: {result}")

docs.title: 2.3.2 Java - Static and Object-Oriented
docs.text:
public class Calculator {
    // Java requires explicit types
    public static int addNumbers(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int a = 15;
        int b = 25;
        int result = addNumbers(a, b);
        System.out.println("The result is: " + result);
    }
}

docs.title: 2.3.3 Haskell - Pure Functional
docs.text:
-- Haskell emphasizes pure functions
addNumbers :: Int -> Int -> Int
addNumbers a b = a + b

main :: IO ()
main = do
    let a = 15
    let b = 25
    let result = addNumbers a b
    putStrLn $ "The result is: " ++ show result

docs.text:
// JavaScript supports multiple styles

// Functional style
const addNumbers = (a, b) => a + b;

// Object-oriented style
class Calculator {
    add(a, b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}

// Usage
const a = 15;
const b = 25;
const result = addNumbers(a, b);
console.log(`The result is: ${result}`);

docs.title: 2.4 Type Systems: The Language’s Contract
docs.text: Type systems define how a language categorizes and constrains values, providing safety and performance benefits.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Static vs Dynamic Typing
docs.text:
Figure 2.2. Static vs Dynamic Typing Trade-offs

Practical Example

Type Safety in Action:

// This won't compile - error caught immediately
int result = "hello" + 5;  // Compile error!

# This runs but may cause runtime error
def process_data(x):
    return x + 5  # Works if x is number, fails if string

process_data(10)      # Works: returns 15
process_data("hello") # Runtime error!

docs.title: 2.5 Language Features and Their Compilation Impact
docs.text: Different language features require different compilation strategies:

docs.title: 2.5.1 Automatic Memory Management
docs.text:
• Garbage Collection (Java, Python): Runtime overhead, unpredictable pauses

  • Reference Counting (Swift, Python): Predictable but can’t handle cycles

  • Manual Management (C, C++): Fast but error-prone

  • Ownership System (Rust): Compile-time safety with no runtime cost

docs.title: 2.5.2 Dynamic Features
docs.text:
# Python's dynamic nature
class_name = input("Enter class name: ")
MyClass = type(class_name, (), {"x": 5})

# Create methods at runtime
setattr(MyClass, "get_x", lambda self: self.x)

# The compiler can't optimize this!
obj = MyClass()
print(obj.get_x())

docs.title: 2.6 From Source Code to Next Stage
docs.text:
Before compilation, your source code is just text. The compiler must:

1. Tokenize: Break text into meaningful symbols 2. Parse: Build a syntax tree 3. Analyze: Check types and semantics 4. Optimize: Improve performance 5. Generate: Produce lower-level code

Solved Problem

Understanding Language Design Trade-offs

Problem: Design a simple expression evaluator that demonstrates the difference between interpreted and compiled execution.

Solution:

class Interpreter:
    def evaluate(self, expression):
        """Evaluate expression directly"""
        # Parse and execute immediately
        tokens = self.tokenize(expression)
        return self.execute(tokens)

    def tokenize(self, expr):
        # Simple tokenization
        return expr.replace('+', ' + ').replace('*', ' * ').split()

    def execute(self, tokens):
        # Direct execution during parsing
        stack = []
        for token in tokens:
            if token.isdigit():
                stack.append(int(token))
            elif token == '+':
                b, a = stack.pop(), stack.pop()
                stack.append(a + b)
            elif token == '*':
                b, a = stack.pop(), stack.pop()
                stack.append(a * b)
        return stack[0]

# Usage
interp = Interpreter()
result = interp.evaluate("3 5 + 2 *")  # (3+5)*2 = 16
print(f"Result: {result}")

class Compiler:
    def compile(self, expression):
        """Compile to bytecode first"""
        tokens = self.tokenize(expression)
        bytecode = self.generate_bytecode(tokens)
        return bytecode

    def tokenize(self, expr):
        return expr.replace('+', ' + ').replace('*', ' * ').split()

    def generate_bytecode(self, tokens):
        """Generate virtual machine instructions"""
        bytecode = []
        for token in tokens:
            if token.isdigit():
                bytecode.append(('PUSH', int(token)))
            elif token == '+':
                bytecode.append(('ADD',))
            elif token == '*':
                bytecode.append(('MUL',))
        return bytecode

    def execute_bytecode(self, bytecode):
        """Virtual machine executes bytecode"""
        stack = []
        for instruction in bytecode:
            if instruction[0] == 'PUSH':
                stack.append(instruction[1])
            elif instruction[0] == 'ADD':
                b, a = stack.pop(), stack.pop()
                stack.append(a + b)
            elif instruction[0] == 'MUL':
                b, a = stack.pop(), stack.pop()
                stack.append(a * b)
        return stack[0]

# Usage
compiler = Compiler()
bytecode = compiler.compile("3 5 + 2 *")
print(f"Bytecode: {bytecode}")
result = compiler.execute_bytecode(bytecode)
print(f"Result: {result}")

Key Insight: The compiled approach separates analysis from execution, allowing optimization and reuse.

docs.title: 2.8 Advanced Topics
docs.text:
Advanced Topic

Just-In-Time (JIT) Compilation:

Modern languages like Java and C# use JIT compilation, combining benefits of interpretation and compilation:

  1. Source code compiles to bytecode (platform-independent)

  2. Bytecode ships to users

  3. JIT compiler translates hot code paths to native machine code

  4. Runtime profiling guides optimization

This approach provides:

  • Platform independence

  • Runtime optimization based on actual usage

  • Reasonable startup time

  • Near-native performance for hot code

docs.title: 2.10 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
High-level programming languages are humanity’s tool for instructing computers while maintaining sanity. They provide:

  • Abstraction: Hide complexity, express intent

  • Productivity: Write less, accomplish more

  • Safety: Catch errors before they cause damage

  • Portability: Run on different hardware

Our simple addition operation (result = a + b) looks trivial in a high-level language, but this simplicity masks enormous complexity. The next chapter explores how compilers bridge the gap between human-friendly code and machine instructions.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Compilation: The Great Translation Process
docs.text: Compilation is the bridge between human thought and machine execution. In this chapter, we dive deep into how compilers transform high-level code into machine instructions, exploring each phase of this remarkable translation process.

docs.title: 3.1 The Compilation Pipeline
docs.text:
A compiler is essentially a translator that converts source code written in a high-level language into target code that can be executed by a machine. This translation happens through multiple phases, each solving a specific problem.

Figure 3.1. The Complete Compilation Pipeline

docs.title: 3.2 Phase 1: Lexical Analysis (Tokenization)
docs.text: The lexer reads the source code character by character and groups them into meaningful units called tokens.

docs.title: 3.2.1 What is a Token?
docs.text:
A token is the smallest meaningful unit in a programming language:

int result = a + b * 2;

This becomes the following token stream:

Token Type Value Category KEYWORD int Type specifier IDENTIFIER result Variable name OPERATOR = Assignment IDENTIFIER a Variable name OPERATOR + Addition IDENTIFIER b Variable name OPERATOR * Multiplication NUMBER 2 Integer literal SEMICOLON ; Statement terminator

Practical Example

Implementing a Simple Lexer:

import re

class Token:
    def __init__(self, type, value):
        self.type = type
        self.value = value

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'Token({self.type}, {self.value})'

class Lexer:
    def __init__(self, text):
        self.text = text
        self.pos = 0
        self.current_char = self.text[0] if text else None

    def advance(self):
        self.pos += 1
        if self.pos >= len(self.text):
            self.current_char = None
        else:
            self.current_char = self.text[self.pos]

    def skip_whitespace(self):
        while self.current_char and self.current_char.isspace():
            self.advance()

    def read_number(self):
        num_str = ''
        while self.current_char and self.current_char.isdigit():
            num_str += self.current_char
            self.advance()
        return int(num_str)

    def read_identifier(self):
        id_str = ''
        while self.current_char and (self.current_char.isalnum() or
                                     self.current_char == '_'):
            id_str += self.current_char
            self.advance()
        return id_str

    def tokenize(self):
        tokens = []
        keywords = {'int', 'float', 'if', 'else', 'while', 'return'}

        while self.current_char:
            if self.current_char.isspace():
                self.skip_whitespace()
            elif self.current_char.isdigit():
                tokens.append(Token('NUMBER', self.read_number()))
            elif self.current_char.isalpha() or self.current_char == '_':
                identifier = self.read_identifier()
                if identifier in keywords:
                    tokens.append(Token('KEYWORD', identifier))
                else:
                    tokens.append(Token('IDENTIFIER', identifier))
            elif self.current_char in '+-*/':
                tokens.append(Token('OPERATOR', self.current_char))
                self.advance()
            elif self.current_char == '=':
                tokens.append(Token('ASSIGN', '='))
                self.advance()
            elif self.current_char == ';':
                tokens.append(Token('SEMICOLON', ';'))
                self.advance()
            else:
                raise ValueError(f'Unexpected character: {self.current_char}')

        return tokens

# Example usage
lexer = Lexer("int result = a + b * 2;")
tokens = lexer.tokenize()
for token in tokens:
    print(token)

docs.title: 3.3 Phase 2: Syntax Analysis (Parsing)
docs.text: The parser takes the token stream and builds an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) that represents the grammatical structure of the program.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Context-Free Grammars
docs.text:
Programming languages are defined by context-free grammars. Here’s a simple grammar for arithmetic expressions:

expression  → term (('+' | '-') term)*
term        → factor (('*' | '/') factor)*
factor      → NUMBER | '(' expression ')'

docs.title: 3.3.2 Building the Abstract Syntax Tree
docs.text:
For our example result = a + b * 2, the AST would look like:

Figure 3.2. Abstract Syntax Tree for result = a + b * 2

Solved Problem

Building a Recursive Descent Parser

Problem: Implement a parser for simple arithmetic expressions that respects operator precedence.

Solution:

class ASTNode:
    pass

class BinaryOp(ASTNode):
    def __init__(self, left, op, right):
        self.left = left
        self.op = op
        self.right = right

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'({self.left} {self.op} {self.right})'

class Number(ASTNode):
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value

    def __repr__(self):
        return str(self.value)

class Parser:
    def __init__(self, tokens):
        self.tokens = tokens
        self.pos = 0
        self.current_token = tokens[0] if tokens else None

    def advance(self):
        self.pos += 1
        if self.pos < len(self.tokens):
            self.current_token = self.tokens[self.pos]
        else:
            self.current_token = None

    def parse_expression(self):
        """expression → term (('+' | '-') term)*"""
        left = self.parse_term()

        while (self.current_token and
               self.current_token.type == 'OPERATOR' and
               self.current_token.value in '+-'):
            op = self.current_token.value
            self.advance()
            right = self.parse_term()
            left = BinaryOp(left, op, right)

        return left

    def parse_term(self):
        """term → factor (('*' | '/') factor)*"""
        left = self.parse_factor()

        while (self.current_token and
               self.current_token.type == 'OPERATOR' and
               self.current_token.value in '*/'):
            op = self.current_token.value
            self.advance()
            right = self.parse_factor()
            left = BinaryOp(left, op, right)

        return left

    def parse_factor(self):
        """factor → NUMBER | '(' expression ')'"""
        token = self.current_token

        if token.type == 'NUMBER':
            self.advance()
            return Number(token.value)
        elif token.value == '(':
            self.advance()
            expr = self.parse_expression()
            if self.current_token.value != ')':
                raise SyntaxError("Expected ')'")
            self.advance()
            return expr
        else:
            raise SyntaxError(f"Unexpected token: {token}")

# Example: Parse "2 + 3 * 4"
lexer = Lexer("2 + 3 * 4")
tokens = lexer.tokenize()
parser = Parser(tokens)
ast = parser.parse_expression()
print(f"AST: {ast}")  # Output: (2 + (3 * 4))

docs.title: 3.4 Phase 3: Semantic Analysis
docs.text: Semantic analysis ensures the program makes sense beyond just having correct syntax. It checks:

docs.title: 3.4.1 Type Checking
docs.text:
// Valid: compatible types
int a = 5;
int b = a + 10;

// Invalid: incompatible types
int x = "hello";  // Error: cannot assign string to int

// Invalid: undeclared variable
y = 20;  // Error: 'y' not declared

docs.title: 3.4.2 Symbol Table Management
docs.text:
The compiler maintains a symbol table to track all identifiers:

Name Type Scope Memory Location Attributes a int global 0x1000 initialized b int global 0x1004 initialized result int global 0x1008 - add_numbers function global 0x2000 returns int

docs.title: 3.5 Phase 4: Intermediate Code Generation
docs.text: The compiler generates an intermediate representation (IR) that’s independent of both the source language and target machine.

docs.title: 3.5.1 Three-Address Code
docs.text:
A common IR format where each instruction has at most three operands:

// Source: result = a + b * 2

t1 = b * 2
t2 = a + t1
result = t2

docs.title: 3.5.2 Static Single Assignment (SSA)
docs.text:
Modern compilers often use SSA form where each variable is assigned exactly once:

// Original code
x = 1
x = x + 1
y = x * 2

// SSA form
x1 = 1
x2 = x1 + 1
y1 = x2 * 2

docs.title: 3.6 Phase 5: Optimization
docs.text: Optimization transforms the IR to improve performance without changing behavior.

docs.title: Constant Folding
docs.text:
// Before optimization
int x = 2 + 3;
int y = x * 4;

// After optimization
int x = 5;      // Computed at compile time
int y = 20;     // Also computed at compile time

docs.title: Dead Code Elimination
docs.text:
// Before optimization
int calculate(int a) {
    int unused = a * 2;  // Never used
    if (false) {
        return 0;        // Unreachable
    }
    return a + 1;
}

// After optimization
int calculate(int a) {
    return a + 1;
}

docs.title: Loop Optimization
docs.text:
// Before optimization
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    int x = a * b;  // Doesn't depend on i
    result[i] = x + i;
}

// After optimization
int x = a * b;  // Moved outside loop
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    result[i] = x + i;
}

Real-World Analogy

Think of compiler optimization like editing a draft essay:

  • Constant folding: Replace "2+2" with "4" throughout

  • Dead code elimination: Remove sentences that don’t contribute

  • Common subexpression: Don’t repeat the same explanation twice

  • Inlining: Replace "see appendix A" with the actual content

docs.title: 3.7 Phase 6: Code Generation
docs.text: Finally, the compiler generates machine code for the target architecture.

docs.title: 3.7.1 Register Allocation
docs.text:
The compiler must map variables to the limited number of CPU registers:

// IR Code
t1 = a + b
t2 = c * d
t3 = t1 + t2

// x86 Assembly (after register allocation)
mov eax, [a]     ; Load a into register eax
add eax, [b]     ; Add b to eax (t1 = a + b)
mov ebx, [c]     ; Load c into register ebx
imul ebx, [d]    ; Multiply ebx by d (t2 = c * d)
add eax, ebx     ; Add ebx to eax (t3 = t1 + t2)
mov [result], eax; Store result

docs.title: 3.7.2 Instruction Selection
docs.text:
Choosing the best machine instructions for each IR operation:

Figure 3.3. Instruction Selection Choices

docs.title: 3.8 Real Compiler Example: GCC
docs.text:
Let’s trace our addition through GCC’s compilation:

# 1. Preprocessing
gcc -E program.c -o program.i

# 2. Compilation to assembly
gcc -S program.i -o program.s

# 3. Assembly to object code
gcc -c program.s -o program.o

# 4. Linking
gcc program.o -o program

# View intermediate representations
gcc -fdump-tree-all program.c  # Dump all IR stages

Practical Example

Examining GCC Output:

// test.c
int main() {
    int a = 15;
    int b = 25;
    int result = a + b;
    return result;
}

.text
    .globl  main
main:
    pushq
    movq
    movl    $15, -4(
    movl    $25, -8(
    movl    -4(
    addl    -8(
    movl
    movl    -12(
    popq
    ret

With optimization (-O2), GCC produces:

main:
    movl    $40,
    ret

docs.text:
Exercise for You

Write a lexer that can tokenize the following C-like code:

if (x > 10) {
    y = x * 2;
} else {
    y = x + 5;
}

Your lexer should identify keywords, operators, identifiers, numbers, and delimiters.

Exercise for You

Test with: x = -(a + b) * 2

Exercise for You

For each code snippet, identify which optimizations could be applied:

// Snippet A
for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
    array[i] = i * 2 * 3;
}

    int a = x * 2;
    int b = x * 2;
    return a + b;

// Snippet C

    printf("Debug mode\n");
}

docs.title: 3.10 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Compilation is a sophisticated translation process that bridges human intent and machine execution. Through six major phases:

1. Lexical Analysis: Text → Tokens 2. Syntax Analysis: Tokens → AST 3. Semantic Analysis: AST → Validated AST 4. IR Generation: AST → Intermediate Code 5. Optimization: IR → Optimized IR 6. Code Generation: IR → Machine Code

Our simple addition (result = a + b) undergoes extensive analysis and transformation, potentially being optimized to a single constant if the values are known at compile time.

Key Takeaway

Key Insight: The compiler is your first and most powerful optimization tool. Understanding how it works helps you write better code and debug mysterious behaviors.

Next: Chapter 4 - Object Files: The Incomplete Puzzle Pieces

docs.title: Chapter 4: Object Files: The Incomplete Puzzle Pieces
docs.text: After compilation, we don’t immediately get an executable program. Instead, we get object files - partially compiled modules that contain machine code but aren’t yet ready to run. This chapter explores these intermediate artifacts and their crucial role in building software.

docs.title: 4.1 What Are Object Files?
docs.text:
Object files are the output of the compilation phase, containing: - Machine code (compiled functions) - Data (global variables, constants) - Symbol information (function and variable names) - Relocation information (how to adjust addresses) - Debug information (if requested)

Think of them as puzzle pieces that need to be assembled to form a complete picture.

Real-World Analogy

Imagine writing a book with multiple authors:

  • Each author writes their chapters independently (source files)

  • Chapters are edited and formatted (compilation)

  • The formatted chapters are not yet a book (object files)

  • An editor combines chapters, adds page numbers, and creates index (linking)

  • The final book is ready to read (executable)

docs.title: 4.2 Object File Formats
docs.text:
Different operating systems use different object file formats:

Format Systems Extensions ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) Linux, Unix .o, .so, .a Mach-O macOS, iOS .o, .dylib, .a PE (Portable Executable) Windows .obj, .dll, .lib COFF (Common Object File Format) Older Unix .o

docs.title: 4.3 Anatomy of an ELF Object File
docs.text:
Let’s examine the most common format: ELF (Executable and Linkable Format).

Figure 4.1. Structure of an ELF Object File

docs.title: 4.3.1 ELF Header
docs.text:
The ELF header identifies the file and provides essential information:

typedef struct {
    unsigned char e_ident[16];  // Magic number and other info
    uint16_t      e_type;       // Object file type
    uint16_t      e_machine;    // Architecture (x86, ARM, etc.)
    uint32_t      e_version;    // File version
    uint64_t      e_entry;      // Entry point address
    uint64_t      e_phoff;      // Program header offset
    uint64_t      e_shoff;      // Section header offset
    uint32_t      e_flags;      // Processor-specific flags
    uint16_t      e_ehsize;     // ELF header size
    uint16_t      e_phentsize;  // Program header entry size
    uint16_t      e_phnum;      // Number of program headers
    uint16_t      e_shentsize;  // Section header entry size
    uint16_t      e_shnum;      // Number of section headers
    uint16_t      e_shstrndx;   // Section name string table index
} Elf64_Ehdr;

docs.title: 4.4 Creating and Examining Object Files
docs.text:
Let’s create object files from our example program:

// math_utils.c
int add_numbers(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

int multiply_numbers(int a, int b) {
    return a * b;
}

// main.c
#include <stdio.h>

// Declaration - tells compiler the function exists
extern int add_numbers(int a, int b);

int main() {
    int result = add_numbers(15, 25);
    printf("Result:
    return 0;
}

# Compile to object files (not executables)
gcc -c math_utils.c -o math_utils.o
gcc -c main.c -o main.o

# Examine object file contents
objdump -h main.o          # Show sections
objdump -t main.o          # Show symbol table
objdump -d main.o          # Disassemble code
objdump -r main.o          # Show relocations
nm main.o                   # List symbols
readelf -a main.o          # Detailed ELF information

docs.title: 4.5 Symbol Tables: The Directory of Contents
docs.text:
The symbol table is like a phone book for the object file, listing all functions and variables:

Practical Example

Symbol Table Example:

$ nm math_utils.o
0000000000000000 T add_numbers
0000000000000015 T multiply_numbers

$ nm main.o
                 U add_numbers
0000000000000000 T main
                 U printf

Symbol types:

  • T: Text (code) section, defined

  • U: Undefined (needs to be linked)

  • D: Data section, defined

  • B: BSS section, defined

  • C: Common (uninitialized data)

docs.title: 4.5.1 Symbol Information Structure
docs.text:
typedef struct {
    uint32_t   st_name;   // Symbol name (index into string table)
    uint8_t    st_info;   // Symbol type and binding
    uint8_t    st_other;  // Symbol visibility
    uint16_t   st_shndx;  // Section index
    uint64_t   st_value;  // Symbol value (address)
    uint64_t   st_size;   // Symbol size
} Elf64_Sym;

docs.title: 4.6 Relocations: Fixing Address References
docs.text: Object files contain placeholders for addresses that will be determined during linking.

docs.title: 4.6.1 Why Relocations Are Needed
docs.text:
When compiling main.c, the compiler doesn’t know: 1. Where add_numbers will be located in memory 2. Where printf will be located 3. The final addresses of global variables

Figure 4.2. Address Resolution During Linking

docs.title: 4.6.2 Relocation Entries
docs.text:
typedef struct {
    uint64_t r_offset;  // Location to apply relocation
    uint64_t r_info;    // Relocation type and symbol index
    int64_t  r_addend;  // Constant addend
} Elf64_Rela;

Solved Problem

Understanding Relocations

Problem: Examine the relocations in an object file and understand what needs to be fixed.

Solution:

$ objdump -r main.o

main.o:     file format elf64-x86-64

RELOCATION RECORDS FOR [.text]:
OFFSET          TYPE              VALUE
000000000000001a R_X86_64_PLT32    add_numbers-0x0000000000000004
000000000000002f R_X86_64_PLT32    printf-0x0000000000000004

RELOCATION RECORDS FOR [.rodata]:
OFFSET          TYPE              VALUE
0000000000000000 R_X86_64_64       .rodata

This tells us: - At offset 0x1a in the code, there’s a call to add_numbers that needs fixing - At offset 0x2f, there’s a call to printf that needs fixing - The R_X86_64_PLT32 type indicates a 32-bit PLT (Procedure Linkage Table) relocation

docs.title: 4.7.1 .text Section: The Code
docs.text:
Contains the compiled machine code:

$ objdump -d math_utils.o

0000000000000000 <add_numbers>:
   0:   55                      push
   1:   48 89 e5                mov
   4:   89 7d fc                mov
   7:   89 75 f8                mov
   a:   8b 45 fc                mov    -0x4(
   d:   03 45 f8                add    -0x8(
  10:   5d                      pop
  11:   c3                      ret

docs.title: 4.7.2 .data Section: Initialized Globals
docs.text:
// These go in .data section
int global_counter = 42;
char message[] = "Hello";
float pi = 3.14159;

docs.title: 4.7.3 .bss Section: Uninitialized Globals
docs.text:
// These go in .bss section (Block Started by Symbol)
int uninitialized_array[1000];  // No initial values
static int counter;             // Implicitly zero
char buffer[8192];              // Large uninitialized buffer

The .bss section doesn’t actually store zeros in the file - it just records how much zero-initialized space is needed.

docs.title: 4.7.4 .rodata Section: Read-Only Data
docs.text:
// These go in .rodata section
const int MAX_SIZE = 100;
const char* greeting = "Hello, World!";
static const double PI = 3.14159265359;

docs.title: 4.8 Static vs Dynamic Libraries
docs.text: Object files can be packaged into libraries:

docs.title: 4.8.1 Static Libraries (.a files)
docs.text:
Archives of object files, linked directly into the executable:

# Create a static library
ar rcs libmath.a math_utils.o other_utils.o

# View contents
ar t libmath.a

# Extract object files
ar x libmath.a

# Link with static library
gcc main.o -L. -lmath -o program
# Or directly:
gcc main.o libmath.a -o program

docs.title: 4.8.2 Dynamic/Shared Libraries (.so files)
docs.text:
Loaded at runtime, shared between programs:

# Create a shared library
gcc -shared -fPIC math_utils.o -o libmath.so

# Link with shared library
gcc main.o -L. -lmath -o program

# View dependencies
ldd program

# Set library path for runtime
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=.:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
./program
Figure 4.3. Static vs Dynamic Library Linking

docs.title: 4.9 Practical Examples
docs.text:
Practical Example

Building a Multi-File Project:

# Project structure:
# main.c - main program
# math_utils.c - math functions
# string_utils.c - string functions
# utils.h - declarations

# Step 1: Compile each source file to object file
gcc -c main.c -o main.o
gcc -c math_utils.c -o math_utils.o
gcc -c string_utils.c -o string_utils.o

# Step 2: Create a static library
ar rcs libutils.a math_utils.o string_utils.o

# Step 3: Link everything together
gcc main.o -L. -lutils -o myprogram

# Examine the final executable
size myprogram      # Show section sizes
strings myprogram   # Extract string literals
objdump -h myprogram # Show all sections

docs.title: 4.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise for You

Exercise 4.1: Object File Analysis

Create a simple C program with: 1. A global initialized variable 2. A global uninitialized array 3. A function that uses a string literal 4. A function that calls an external function

Compile to an object file and identify which section each element belongs to.

Exercise for You

Exercise 4.2: Symbol Resolution

Given these files:

// file1.c
int shared_var = 10;
void func1() { shared_var++; }

// file2.c
extern int shared_var;
void func2() { shared_var--; }

// main.c

extern void func2();
int main() { func1(); func2(); return 0; }

1. Compile each to object files 2. Examine the symbol tables 3. Identify which symbols are undefined in each file 4. Predict how the linker will resolve them

Exercise for You

Exercise 4.3: Library Creation

Create both static and dynamic versions of a simple library that provides: - String reversal function - String length function - String concatenation function

Write a test program that uses all three functions. Compare the size of executables linked with static vs dynamic libraries.

docs.title: 4.11 Advanced Topics
docs.text:
Advanced Topic

Position Independent Code (PIC):

Shared libraries must work at any memory address, requiring special compilation:

# Compile with PIC for shared libraries
gcc -fPIC -c math_utils.c

# Why PIC matters:
# Without PIC: call 0x401000  (absolute address)
# With PIC:    call [GOT+offset] (relative addressing)

PIC uses the Global Offset Table (GOT) and Procedure Linkage Table (PLT) for indirection, allowing the same code to work regardless of where it’s loaded in memory.

docs.title: 4.12 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Object files are the crucial intermediate step between source code and executables:

  • They contain compiled code but with unresolved references

  • Symbol tables track all functions and variables

  • Relocation entries mark addresses that need fixing

  • Different sections organize code, data, and metadata

  • Libraries package object files for reuse

Our simple addition function exists as machine code in the .text section, with its symbol in the symbol table, waiting to be connected with the rest of the program.

Key Takeaway

Key Insight: Object files enable separate compilation - a fundamental feature that makes large software projects manageable. Without them, we’d have to recompile everything for every change!

Next: Chapter 5 - Linking: Connecting the Puzzle Pieces

docs.title: Chapter 5: Linking: Connecting the Puzzle Pieces
docs.text: Linking is the final step in building an executable program. The linker takes object files and libraries, resolves all symbolic references, and produces a complete program ready to run. This chapter explores how scattered pieces become a unified whole.

docs.title: 5.1 The Linker’s Job
docs.text:
The linker (ld on Unix systems) performs several critical tasks:

  1. Symbol Resolution: Match undefined symbols with their definitions

  2. Relocation: Adjust code and data addresses to their final locations

  3. Section Merging: Combine sections from multiple object files

  4. Library Processing: Include needed functions from libraries

  5. Entry Point Setting: Determine where program execution begins

Figure 5.1. The Linking Process

docs.title: 5.2 Symbol Resolution
docs.text: Symbol resolution matches every undefined reference with exactly one definition.

docs.title: 5.2.1 Symbol Types and Binding
docs.text: Symbol Type Binding Description Strong Symbol Global Functions and initialized globals Weak Symbol Global Uninitialized globals Local Symbol Local Static functions and variables External Symbol External Defined in another file

docs.title: 5.2.2 Symbol Resolution Rules
docs.text:
1. Rule 1: Multiple strong symbols with the same name → Error

  2. Rule 2: One strong symbol and multiple weak symbols → Choose strong

  3. Rule 3: Multiple weak symbols → Choose any (usually largest)

Solved Problem

Symbol Resolution Examples

Problem: Predict the outcome of linking these files:

// strong.c
int x = 10;           // Strong symbol
int y;                // Weak symbol
void func() {         // Strong symbol
    x = 20;
}

// weak.c
int x;                // Weak symbol - OK, strong wins
int y = 5;            // Strong symbol - OK, was weak
void func();          // External reference - OK
int main() {
    func();
    return x + y;
}

Solution: - x: Strong symbol from strong.c (value 10, then 20 after func()) - y: Strong symbol from weak.c (value 5) - func: Defined in strong.c, used in weak.c - Links successfully!

But this would fail:

// file1.c
int data = 10;  // Strong symbol

// file2.c
int data = 20;  // Strong symbol - ERROR! Multiple definitions

docs.title: 5.3 Address Space and Memory Layout
docs.text:
The linker arranges the program in memory according to a specific layout:

Figure 5.2. Typical Process Memory Layout (Linux x86-64)

docs.title: 5.4 Relocation Process
docs.text: Relocation adjusts addresses in the code to reflect the final memory layout.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Two-Pass Algorithm
docs.text:
Pass 1: Section Merging and Address Assignment

// Merge sections from all object files
.text_final = merge(main.o:.text, math.o:.text, util.o:.text)
.data_final = merge(main.o:.data, math.o:.data, util.o:.data)

// Assign addresses
text_start = 0x400000
data_start = text_start + sizeof(.text_final)
bss_start = data_start + sizeof(.data_final)

// Build symbol table with final addresses
for each symbol in all_object_files:
    symbol.address = section_base + symbol.offset

Pass 2: Relocation Application

for each relocation in all_object_files:
    target_addr = symbol_table[relocation.symbol].address
    patch_location = section_base + relocation.offset

    switch(relocation.type):
        case R_X86_64_32:
            *patch_location = target_addr
        case R_X86_64_PC32:
            *patch_location = target_addr - patch_location - 4
        // ... other relocation types

Practical Example

Relocation in Action:

Before linking (main.o):

0000000000000015 <main>:
  ...
  1a:   e8 00 00 00 00    call 1f <main+0xa>  # Placeholder
  1f:   ...

Relocation entry:

Offset: 0x1a+1  Type: R_X86_64_PLT32  Symbol: add_numbers

After linking (executable):

0000000000401015 <main>:
  ...
  40101a:   e8 24 00 00 00    call 401043 <add_numbers>
  40101f:   ...

0000000000401043 <add_numbers>:
  ...

The call instruction now has the correct relative offset (0x24) to reach add_numbers.

docs.title: 5.5 Static Linking
docs.text: Static linking copies all required code into the final executable.

docs.title: 5.5.1 Library Archive Processing
docs.text:
# Create object files
gcc -c file1.c -o file1.o
gcc -c file2.c -o file2.o
gcc -c file3.c -o file3.o

# Create static library
ar rcs libmylib.a file1.o file2.o file3.o

# Link with library
gcc main.o -L. -lmylib -o program
# Equivalent to:
gcc main.o libmylib.a -o program

# The linker:
# 1. Scans main.o for undefined symbols
# 2. Searches libmylib.a for definitions
# 3. Extracts only needed object files from library
# 4. Includes them in final executable

docs.title: 5.5.2 Link Order Matters
docs.text:
Real-World Analogy

Think of linking like following recipe dependencies:

  • You can’t frost a cake before baking it

  • You can’t reference a function before the linker has seen it

  • Libraries should come after the files that need them

# WRONG - library before object that needs it
gcc -lm main.o -o program  # math library before main.o

# CORRECT - library after object that needs it
gcc main.o -lm -o program  # main.o needs math library

# Multiple library dependencies
gcc main.o -lgraphics -lmath -lbase -o program
# If graphics needs math, and math needs base, this order works

docs.title: 5.6 Dynamic Linking
docs.text: Dynamic linking defers symbol resolution until runtime.

docs.title: 5.6.1 Advantages and Disadvantages
docs.text: Advantages Disadvantages Smaller executables Runtime overhead Shared library updates Dependency management Memory efficiency "DLL Hell" potential Plugin architectures Deployment complexity

docs.title: Procedure Linkage Table (PLT)
docs.text:
The PLT provides lazy binding - functions are resolved on first call:

Figure 5.3. PLT and GOT Interaction

docs.title: Global Offset Table (GOT)
docs.text:
The GOT holds addresses of global symbols:

# First call to printf
printf@plt:
    jmp    *printf@got(
    pushq  $0                    # Push symbol ID
    jmp    .plt0                 # Jump to resolver

# After resolution, GOT contains actual printf address
# Subsequent calls jump directly to printf

docs.title: 5.7 The Dynamic Linker/Loader
docs.text:
The dynamic linker (ld.so on Linux) runs before main():

1. Kernel loads program and ld.so
2. ld.so gains control before main()
3. ld.so:
   - Loads required shared libraries
   - Resolves symbols (lazy or immediate)
   - Performs relocations
   - Initializes libraries
4. Control transfers to main()

Practical Example

Examining Dynamic Dependencies:

# View dynamic dependencies
$ ldd ./program
    linux-vdso.so.1 =>  (0x00007ffd3d5f0000)
    libc.so.6 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 (0x00007f823d200000)
    /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 (0x00007f823d600000)

# View dynamic symbols
$ nm -D program
                 U printf@@GLIBC_2.2.5
                 U __libc_start_main@@GLIBC_2.2.5
0000000000401050 T main

# Trace dynamic linking
$ LD_DEBUG=all ./program 2>&1 | head -20

docs.title: 5.8 Linker Scripts
docs.text:
Linker scripts control the linking process in detail:

ENTRY(_start)  /* Entry point */

SECTIONS
{
    . = 0x400000;  /* Start address */

    .text : {
        *(.text)   /* All .text sections */
        *(.rodata) /* All .rodata sections */
    }

    . = ALIGN(0x1000);  /* Align to page boundary */

    .data : {
        *(.data)   /* All .data sections */
    }

    .bss : {
        *(.bss)    /* All .bss sections */
        *(COMMON)  /* Common symbols */
    }

    /DISCARD/ : {
        *(.comment) /* Discard comment sections */
    }
}

docs.title: 5.9.1 Undefined Reference
docs.text:
$ gcc main.o -o program
main.o: In function `main':
main.c:(.text+0x15): undefined reference to `add_numbers'

# Solution: Include the missing object file or library
$ gcc main.o math.o -o program

docs.title: 5.9.2 Multiple Definition
docs.text:
// header.h
int global = 10;  // WRONG - definition in header

// Better:
// header.h
extern int global;  // Declaration only

// one_file.c
int global = 10;    // Single definition

docs.title: 5.9.3 Library Not Found
docs.text:
$ gcc main.o -lmylib -o program
/usr/bin/ld: cannot find -lmylib

# Solutions:
# 1. Specify library path
$ gcc main.o -L/path/to/lib -lmylib -o program

# 2. Set environment variable
$ export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/path/to/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

# 3. Install in system directory
$ sudo cp libmylib.so /usr/local/lib/
$ sudo ldconfig

docs.title: 5.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise for You

Exercise 5.1: Symbol Resolution Challenge

Given these files, predict what the linker will do:

// strong.c
int x = 1;
int y = 2;

// weak.c

float y;  // Type mismatch!

// main.c

extern float y;
int main() {
    return x + (int)y;
}

Compile and link them. What happens? Why?

Exercise for You

Exercise 5.2: Custom Linker Script

Write a linker script that: 1. Places code at address 0x500000 2. Ensures data section is 4KB aligned 3. Creates a custom section for configuration data 4. Defines symbols for section start/end addresses

Test with a simple program that uses these features.

Exercise for You

Exercise 5.3: Dynamic Linking Investigation

1. Create a shared library with three functions 2. Write a program that uses only one function 3. Use LD_DEBUG to observe the linking process 4. Compare PLT/GOT contents before and after first function call 5. Measure the overhead of dynamic vs static linking

docs.title: 5.11 Advanced Topics
docs.text:
Advanced Topic

Link-Time Optimization (LTO):

Modern linkers can optimize across compilation units:

# Compile with LTO
gcc -flto -c file1.c -o file1.o
gcc -flto -c file2.c -o file2.o

# Link with LTO - linker can now:
# - Inline functions across files
# - Remove unused code globally
# - Optimize based on whole program
gcc -flto file1.o file2.o -o program

LTO enables optimizations impossible during separate compilation, at the cost of longer link times.

docs.title: 5.12 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Linking transforms a collection of object files into a complete executable:

  • Symbol Resolution: Matches references with definitions

  • Relocation: Assigns final addresses and patches code

  • Section Merging: Combines similar sections from all inputs

  • Static Linking: Creates self-contained executables

  • Dynamic Linking: Defers library binding to runtime

Our simple addition function, compiled in math_utils.o, is finally connected to main() and assigned its permanent address in the executable. The program is now ready to be loaded and run!

Key Takeaway

Key Insight: Linking is where separate compilation’s promise is fulfilled - allowing modular development while creating efficient executables. It’s the bridge between development flexibility and runtime performance.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Program Loading: Bringing Code to Life
docs.text: When you double-click an executable or type its name in a terminal, a complex dance begins. The operating system must transform a dormant file on disk into a living process in memory. This chapter explores how programs come to life through the loading process.

docs.title: 6.1 From File to Process
docs.text:
A program on disk is just data - organized, structured, but lifeless. Loading transforms it into an active process with: - Memory space allocated - Code and data properly positioned - CPU state initialized - Resources allocated - Execution ready to begin

Figure 6.1. Program Loading: From Disk to Memory

docs.title: 6.2 The Boot Process: Before Your Program
docs.text: Before any user program can run, the system itself must boot:

docs.title: 6.2.1 System Initialization
docs.text:
1. BIOS/UEFI: Hardware initialization

  2. Bootloader: Loads the operating system kernel

  3. Kernel: Initializes memory management, drivers, filesystems

  4. Init Process: First user-space process (PID 1)

  5. System Services: Network, logging, device management

  6. Login/Shell: Ready for user programs

docs.title: 6.3 The Executable Format: Reading the Blueprint
6.3.1 ELF Header Revisited
docs.text:
The loader’s first job is to read and validate the executable:

typedef struct {
    unsigned char e_ident[16];  // Magic number: 0x7F 'E' 'L' 'F'
    uint16_t      e_type;       // ET_EXEC (executable) or ET_DYN (shared)
    uint16_t      e_machine;    // Target architecture (x86_64, ARM, etc.)
    uint64_t      e_entry;      // Entry point address (where to start)
    uint64_t      e_phoff;      // Program header table offset
    uint16_t      e_phnum;      // Number of program headers
} Elf64_Ehdr;

docs.title: 6.3.2 Program Headers: The Loading Instructions
docs.text:
While section headers were for linking, program headers are for loading:

typedef struct {
    uint32_t p_type;    // Segment type (LOAD, DYNAMIC, INTERP...)
    uint32_t p_flags;   // Permissions (R, W, X)
    uint64_t p_offset;  // File offset
    uint64_t p_vaddr;   // Virtual address in memory
    uint64_t p_paddr;   // Physical address (usually ignored)
    uint64_t p_filesz;  // Size in file
    uint64_t p_memsz;   // Size in memory (may be larger)
    uint64_t p_align;   // Alignment requirement
} Elf64_Phdr;

Practical Example

Examining Program Headers:

$ readelf -l program

Program Headers:
  Type           Offset   VirtAddr           PhysAddr           FileSiz  MemSiz   Flg Align
  PHDR           0x000040 0x0000000000400040 0x0000000000400040 0x0001f8 0x0001f8 R   0x8
  INTERP         0x000238 0x0000000000400238 0x0000000000400238 0x00001c 0x00001c R   0x1
      [Requesting program interpreter: /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2]
  LOAD           0x000000 0x0000000000400000 0x0000000000400000 0x000794 0x000794 R E 0x200000
  LOAD           0x000e00 0x0000000000600e00 0x0000000000600e00 0x000230 0x000238 RW  0x200000
  DYNAMIC        0x000e10 0x0000000000600e10 0x0000000000600e10 0x0001d0 0x0001d0 RW  0x8
  NOTE           0x000254 0x0000000000400254 0x0000000000400254 0x000044 0x000044 R   0x4
  GNU_STACK      0x000000 0x0000000000000000 0x0000000000000000 0x000000 0x000000 RW  0x10

docs.title: 6.4 The Loading Algorithm
docs.text:
The kernel’s exec() system call performs the actual loading:

1. Open executable file
2. Read and validate ELF header
3. Check architecture compatibility
4. Set up new address space
5. For each LOAD segment:
   a. Allocate virtual memory at p_vaddr
   b. Set permissions from p_flags
   c. Copy p_filesz bytes from file
   d. Zero-fill remaining p_memsz - p_filesz bytes
6. Set up stack
7. Handle dynamic linking if needed
8. Set instruction pointer to e_entry
9. Begin execution

docs.title: 6.5 Memory Mapping: Efficient Loading
docs.text: Modern systems use memory mapping for efficient loading:

docs.title: 6.5.1 Copy-on-Write (COW)
docs.text:
Multiple processes can share read-only pages:

Figure 6.2. Copy-on-Write Memory Sharing

docs.title: 6.5.2 Demand Paging
docs.text:
Pages are loaded only when accessed:

1. Program starts with minimal pages loaded
2. CPU accesses unmapped address
3. Page fault exception occurs
4. OS page fault handler:
   a. Determines if access is valid
   b. Allocates physical page
   c. Loads content from disk if needed
   d. Updates page table
   e. Returns to program
5. Instruction retries successfully

docs.title: 6.6 Stack Initialization
docs.text: Before main() runs, the stack must be prepared:

docs.title: 6.6.1 Initial Stack Layout
6.7 Dynamic Loading
docs.text: For dynamically linked programs, additional steps are needed:

docs.title: 6.7.1 The Interpreter
docs.text:
The INTERP program header specifies the dynamic linker:

1. Kernel loads the program
2. Kernel sees INTERP header
3. Kernel loads dynamic linker (ld.so)
4. Control transfers to ld.so, not the program
5. ld.so:
   a. Loads required shared libraries
   b. Performs relocations
   c. Initializes libraries
   d. Transfers control to program's entry point

docs.title: 6.7.2 Library Search Process
docs.text:
The dynamic linker searches for libraries in order:

  1. RPATH in executable (deprecated)

  2. LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable

  3. RUNPATH in executable

  4. /etc/ld.so.cache (cached library locations)

  5. Default paths (/lib, /usr/lib)

Practical Example

Tracing Dynamic Loading:

# See library dependencies
$ ldd ./program
    linux-vdso.so.1 (0x00007fff887dd000)
    libc.so.6 => /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 (0x00007f9a0c000000)
    /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 (0x00007f9a0c400000)

# Trace library loading
$ LD_DEBUG=libs ./program
      1234:     find library=libc.so.6 [0]; searching
      1234:      search cache=/etc/ld.so.cache
      1234:       trying file=/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6
      1234:     calling init: /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6

# Preload a library
$ LD_PRELOAD=./mylib.so ./program

docs.title: 6.8 Process Creation: fork() and exec()
docs.text: Unix systems separate process creation from program loading:

docs.title: 6.8.1 The fork() System Call
docs.text:
Creates an exact copy of the current process:

#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>

int main() {
    printf("Parent PID:

    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid < 0) {
        perror("fork failed");
        return 1;
    } else if (pid == 0) {
        // Child process
        printf("Child PID:
        // Child continues here
    } else {
        // Parent process
        printf("Parent: Created child
        wait(NULL);  // Wait for child
    }

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 6.8.2 The exec() Family
docs.text:
Replaces the current process with a new program:

#include <unistd.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int main() {
    printf("About to exec...\n");

    // Different exec variants:
    // execl:  list arguments
    // execv:  vector of arguments
    // execle: list with environment
    // execve: vector with environment (system call)
    // execlp: search PATH
    // execvp: vector, search PATH

    char *args[] = {"ls", "-l", "/tmp", NULL};

    execvp("ls", args);  // This replaces our program!

    // Only reached if exec fails
    perror("exec failed");
    return 1;
}

docs.title: 6.8.3 The Complete Picture: Shell Launching a Program
docs.text:
int launch_program(char *program, char *args[]) {
    pid_t pid = fork();

    if (pid == 0) {
        // Child: become the new program
        execvp(program, args);
        perror("exec failed");
        exit(1);
    } else if (pid > 0) {
        // Parent: wait for child
        int status;
        waitpid(pid, &status, 0);
        return WEXITSTATUS(status);
    } else {
        perror("fork failed");
        return -1;
    }
}

docs.title: 6.9.1 Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR)
docs.text:
Modern systems randomize memory layout to prevent exploits:

# Run program multiple times, observe different addresses
$ ./program
Stack variable at: 0x7ffd8c9a4520

$ ./program
Stack variable at: 0x7fff2d8b1520  # Different address!

# Disable ASLR (for debugging)
$ echo 0 | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space

# Enable ASLR (default)
$ echo 2 | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space

docs.title: 6.9.2 Executable Space Protection
docs.text:
Modern CPUs support NX (No eXecute) bit:

Real-World Analogy

Think of memory protection like room access in a building:

  • Read: You can look into the room

  • Write: You can modify things in the room

  • Execute: You can perform activities in the room

Code sections are like classrooms (read+execute), data sections are like storage (read+write), and the stack traditionally was both, but modern systems prevent execution for security.

docs.title: 6.10 The C Runtime: Before main()
docs.text:
Before main() runs, the C runtime performs initialization:

// Simplified _start function (actual entry point)
void _start() {
    // 1. Set up initial stack frame
    // 2. Initialize thread local storage
    // 3. Initialize heap allocator
    // 4. Set up standard I/O
    // 5. Register cleanup functions
    // 6. Call global constructors

    // Finally call main
    int result = main(argc, argv, envp);

    // 7. Call global destructors
    // 8. Flush I/O buffers
    // 9. Call exit with result
    exit(result);
}

docs.title: 6.12 Chapter Summary
docs.text:
Program loading transforms static files into living processes:

  • ELF parsing: Headers guide the loading process

  • Memory setup: Virtual address space is created

  • Segment loading: Code and data are mapped

  • Dynamic linking: Libraries are loaded and bound

  • Stack initialization: Arguments and environment prepared

  • Control transfer: Execution begins at entry point

Our simple addition function, now loaded at a specific address in memory, is ready for the CPU to execute. The stage is set for computation to begin!

Key Takeaway

Key Insight: Loading is where the OS takes control, transforming passive files into active processes. It’s the boundary between storage and execution, between potential and action.

docs.title: Chapter 7: CPU Execution & ISA: The Hardware/Software Interface
docs.text: The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the contract between software and hardware - the vocabulary through which programs communicate with processors. This chapter explores how CPUs execute instructions and how our high-level addition becomes concrete machine operations.

docs.title: 7.1 The Instruction Set Architecture
docs.text:
The ISA defines everything software needs to know about the processor: - Available instructions and their encodings - Registers and their purposes - Memory addressing modes - Data types and sizes - Exception and interrupt handling

Figure 7.1. ISA: The Hardware/Software Boundary

docs.title: 7.2.1 x86-64 (Intel/AMD)
docs.text: - CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) - Variable-length instructions (1-15 bytes) - Rich addressing modes - Backwards compatible to 1978 - Dominates desktops and servers

docs.title: 7.2.2 ARM
docs.text: - RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) - Fixed-length instructions (32-bit in ARM, 16/32 in Thumb) - Load/store architecture - Energy efficient - Dominates mobile devices

docs.title: 7.2.3 RISC-V
docs.text:
- Open-source ISA - Modular design - Fixed 32-bit instructions (with 16-bit compressed) - Growing in embedded and academic use

Practical Example

Same Operation, Different ISAs:

Our addition result = a + b in different assembly languages:

; x86-64 (Intel syntax)
mov  eax, [a]      ; Load a into register eax
add  eax, [b]      ; Add b to eax
mov  [result], eax ; Store eax to result

@ ARM assembly
ldr  r0, =a        @ Load address of a
ldr  r1, [r0]      @ Load value of a into r1
ldr  r0, =b        @ Load address of b
ldr  r2, [r0]      @ Load value of b into r2
add  r3, r1, r2    @ Add r1 and r2, store in r3
ldr  r0, =result   @ Load address of result
str  r3, [r0]      @ Store r3 to result

# RISC-V assembly
lw   t0, a         # Load word from a into t0
lw   t1, b         # Load word from b into t1
add  t2, t0, t1    # Add t0 and t1, store in t2
sw   t2, result    # Store t2 to result

docs.title: 7.3 CPU Components
docs.text:
A modern CPU contains several key components:

Figure 7.2. Basic CPU Components

docs.title: 7.3.1 Registers: The CPU’s Workspace
docs.text:
Registers are the fastest storage in the computer:

Register Type Purpose x86-64 Example Access Time General Purpose Computation RAX, RBX, RCX... <1 cycle Stack Pointer Stack top RSP <1 cycle Instruction Pointer Next instruction RIP <1 cycle Flags/Status Condition codes RFLAGS <1 cycle Segment Memory segments CS, DS, SS... <1 cycle

docs.title: 7.4 The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle
docs.text:
The fundamental operation of every CPU:

Figure 7.3. The Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle

docs.title: 7.4.1 Detailed Cycle Steps
docs.text:
Solved Problem

Tracing an ADD Instruction

Problem: Trace the execution of ADD R1, R2, R3 (R1 = R2 + R3)

Solution:

// FETCH PHASE
1. Read Program Counter (PC): 0x1000
2. Send address 0x1000 to memory
3. Memory returns instruction: 0x00430820 (ADD R1, R2, R3)
4. Store instruction in Instruction Register (IR)
5. Increment PC to 0x1004

// DECODE PHASE
6. Decode instruction 0x00430820:
   - Opcode: 000000 (R-type instruction)
   - Rs: 00010 (R2)
   - Rt: 00011 (R3)
   - Rd: 00001 (R1)
   - Function: 100000 (ADD)
7. Read R2 value: 15
8. Read R3 value: 25

// EXECUTE PHASE
9. ALU operation: 15 + 25 = 40
10. Write 40 to R1
11. Update flags if needed (overflow, zero, etc.)
12. Continue to next instruction (PC = 0x1004)

Timing: Modern CPUs can overlap these phases using pipelining, executing multiple instructions simultaneously at different stages.

docs.title: 7.5.1 x86-64 Instruction Encoding
docs.text:
x86-64 uses variable-length encoding:

Figure 7.4. x86-64 Instruction Format

docs.title: 7.5.2 RISC-V Instruction Formats
docs.text:
RISC-V uses fixed 32-bit formats:

// R-Type (Register-Register operations)
31      25 24   20 19   15 14  12 11    7 6       0
[ funct7 ] [  rs2 ] [ rs1 ] [f3] [  rd  ] [ opcode ]
    7         5        5      3      5         7     bits

// I-Type (Immediate operations)
31                20 19   15 14  12 11    7 6       0
[    immediate    ] [ rs1 ] [f3] [  rd  ] [ opcode ]
        12            5      3      5         7     bits

// S-Type (Store operations)
31      25 24   20 19   15 14  12 11    7 6       0
[  imm  ] [  rs2 ] [ rs1 ] [f3] [ imm  ] [ opcode ]
    7         5        5      3      5         7     bits

docs.title: 7.6 Pipelining: Parallel Execution
docs.text:
Modern CPUs pipeline instructions for throughput:

Figure 7.5. 5-Stage Pipeline Execution

docs.title: 7.6.1 Pipeline Hazards
docs.text: Three types of hazards can stall the pipeline:

docs.title: Data Hazards
docs.text:
ADD R1, R2, R3   ; R1 = R2 + R3
SUB R4, R1, R5   ; R4 = R1 - R5 (needs R1 from previous instruction!)

docs.title: Control Hazards
docs.text:
CMP R1, R2       ; Compare R1 and R2
BEQ label        ; Branch if equal (don't know where to fetch next!)

docs.title: Structural Hazards
docs.text: Two instructions need the same hardware resource simultaneously.

docs.title: 7.7.1 Superscalar Execution
docs.text:
Modern CPUs can execute multiple instructions per cycle:

// These independent instructions can execute simultaneously:
ADD R1, R2, R3   ; Uses ALU 1
MUL R4, R5, R6   ; Uses ALU 2
LOAD R7, [R8]    ; Uses Load/Store Unit

// CPU with 2 ALUs and 1 Load/Store unit can do all three in parallel!

docs.title: 7.7.2 Out-of-Order Execution
docs.text:
CPUs can reorder instructions for efficiency:

// Original program order:
1: LOAD R1, [memory1]    ; Slow - cache miss
2: ADD R2, R3, R4        ; Fast - no dependencies
3: MUL R5, R6, R7        ; Fast - no dependencies
4: ADD R8, R1, R9        ; Needs R1 from instruction 1

// Actual execution order:
1: LOAD R1, [memory1]    ; Start load (takes many cycles)
2: ADD R2, R3, R4        ; Execute while waiting
3: MUL R5, R6, R7        ; Execute while waiting
4: ADD R8, R1, R9        ; Execute when R1 ready

docs.title: 7.7.3 Branch Prediction
docs.text:
CPUs predict branch outcomes to avoid stalls:

Real-World Analogy

Branch prediction is like predicting traffic patterns:

  • Static: "This road is usually busy at 5pm" (compile-time hints)

  • Dynamic: "It was busy yesterday and today, so probably tomorrow" (runtime history)

  • Speculative: "I’ll take the highway assuming it’s clear" (execute assuming prediction)

  • Recovery: "Traffic jam! Turn around and take surface streets" (misprediction penalty)

docs.title: 7.8 Memory Hierarchy
docs.text:
CPUs use multiple levels of cache to bridge the speed gap:

Level Size Latency Location Registers 1 KB <1 cycle CPU Core L1 Cache 32-64 KB 3-4 cycles CPU Core L2 Cache 256-512 KB 10-20 cycles CPU Core L3 Cache 8-32 MB 30-40 cycles CPU Die Main Memory 8-64 GB 100-300 cycles DIMM SSD 256GB-2TB 10,000+ cycles PCIe/SATA HDD 1-20 TB 1,000,000+ cycles SATA

Practical Example

Cache Performance Impact:

// Cache-friendly: Sequential access
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    sum += array[i];  // Accesses memory sequentially
}

// Cache-unfriendly: Random access
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    sum += array[random()
}

// Performance difference can be 10-100x!

docs.title: 7.9 SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data
docs.text:
Modern CPUs can operate on multiple data items simultaneously:

// Traditional (4 instructions):
result[0] = a[0] + b[0];
result[1] = a[1] + b[1];
result[2] = a[2] + b[2];
result[3] = a[3] + b[3];

// SIMD (1 instruction):
__m128 va = _mm_load_ps(a);      // Load 4 floats
__m128 vb = _mm_load_ps(b);      // Load 4 floats
__m128 vr = _mm_add_ps(va, vb);  // Add all 4 pairs at once!
_mm_store_ps(result, vr);        // Store 4 results

docs.title: 7.10 Real CPU Example: Intel Core i7
docs.text:
Let’s examine a real modern processor:

Architecture:       x86-64
Cores:             8 physical (16 logical with Hyper-Threading)
Pipeline Depth:    14-19 stages
Issue Width:       4-6 micro-ops per cycle
Execution Units:
  - 4 Integer ALUs
  - 2 Vector ALUs
  - 2 Load units
  - 1 Store unit
Caches:
  - L1I: 32KB per core (instruction)
  - L1D: 32KB per core (data)
  - L2:  256KB per core
  - L3:  16MB shared
Clock Speed:       3.6 GHz base, 5.0 GHz turbo
Transistors:       ~2 billion

docs.text:

Test with various instruction sequences.
